plan.geometry_notes: Long diagonal composition matching the source: the radio source sits at the lower left and the ray bundle rises toward the upper right. Use no coordinate axes and no grid. World-space source S = (0, 0, 0). Central beam direction u = normalize(1.0, 0.55, 0.16). Near distance r1 = 2.25 units; default far distance r2 = 5.2 units. Near patch center C1 = S + r1*u; far patch center C2 = S + r2*u. Near square side s1 = 0.48 units. Far square side must scale as s2 = s1*(r2/r1), so at default r2 = 5.2 the far side is about 1.11 units and A2/A1 is about 5.34. Both squares are perpendicular to the central beam direction and share the same orientation; choose local patch axes perpendicular to u so the visible square appears as a tilted parallelogram, with the top edge slanting slightly downward to the right and the side edges slanting up-left/down-right as in the reference. The four solid rays run exactly from S to the four A1 corners. The four dashed extensions run exactly from each A1 corner to the corresponding A2 corner. The shorter r1 arrow lies below and parallel to the ray bundle, offset about 0.42 world units downward from the beam; it runs from the source projection to the near patch level. The longer r2 arrow lies slightly farther below, offset about 0.72 world units downward; it runs from the source projection to the far patch level. Put 'r1' centered under the shorter arrow and 'r2' centered under the longer arrow. Put 'A1' just above/right of the near patch with a curved arrow pointing to the patch face. Put 'A2' just above/right of the far patch with a curved arrow pointing to the far patch face. Colors: rays and patch outlines medium blue #4f9fc6; patch fill pale blue #a9d2df at 55-65% opacity; dashed continuation rays same blue with a clear dash-gap pattern; labels, arrows, dimension lines, ticks, and leader line black #111111; source dot black #000000. White background. Frame the whole figure so the source-to-A2 diagonal occupies roughly 80-85% of the canvas width and 60-70% of the canvas height, leaving modest room for labels.
plan.notes: Default render must show the complete static reference figure: both A1 and A2, both distance arrows r1 and r2, the dashed ray extensions, and the exact labels 'Radio source', 'A1', 'A2', 'r1', and 'r2'. Do not show formulas, numeric area ratios, intensity labels, or color-coded intensity by default. The constructionStage state only hides/reveals existing reference elements: sourceOnly shows the source dot, label, and leader; nearPatchA1 adds the four solid rays, A1, A1 label/arrow, and r1 arrow; complete shows all default reference elements. The farDistanceR2 slider moves only the far square A2, dashed extensions, r2 arrow endpoint, and A2/r2 label anchors; keep the default value at the reference-like r2 position. Keep the far labels as 'A2' and 'r2' even when the slider is moved. The areaGuide toggle reveals the supplementary A2/A1 relation and side-length guide marks only; do not include inverse-square intensity text or numeric intensity readouts. Use CSS2D or high-resolution sprite text for labels so they remain readable during orbiting.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a perspective diagram of radiation spreading outward from a point source. At the lower left, a small black dot is tied by a wavy leader to the label Radio source. Four solid blue lines fan out from that dot toward the upper right and meet the corners of a small blue-shaded quadrilateral, drawn as a square patch tilted across the beam and labeled A1 by a curved arrow. The same lines continue past it as dashed blue segments and terminate on the corners of a second shaded square farther along the identical direction, noticeably larger and labeled A2. Beneath and parallel to the fan, two long arrows measure distance from the source: the shorter, labeled r1, ends level with the near patch, and the longer, labeled r2, reaches the far one. Because both patches are cut from the same fixed bundle of rays, the growth in area from A1 to A2 set against the growth in distance from r1 to r2 is the comparison on offer. The sketch supports reasoning that a transmitter's power spreads over an area increasing with distance, fixing how intensity and maximum field strength fall off.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for distance r: the learner drags the receiving patch outward along the ray bundle, the square area expands from A1 toward A2 and an intensity readout falls, showing that the same power spreads over area that grows with distance.
- Toggle between area and intensity overlays: the learner switches labels from A(r) to I(r), the patch-size annotation changes to an inverse-square intensity annotation, connecting geometric spreading to the decrease in received signal strength.
authoredContext:
Radio Range A 60-kW radio transmitter on Earth sends its signal to a satellite 100 km away (the figure). At what distance in the same direction would the signal have the same maximum field strength if the transmitter’s output power were increased to 90 kW?

In three dimensions, a signal spreads over a solid angle as it travels outward from its source.

A point is labeled radio source. A small square labeled A1 is in the path of the lines radiating from the radio source. The lines continue from the corners of A1 and reach A2, a slightly bigger square. A1 is at a distance r1 from the source and A2 is at a distance R2.

Strategy The area over which the power in a particular direction is dispersed increases as distance squared, as illustrated in the figure. Change the power output P by a factor of (90 kW/60 kW) and change the area by the same factor to keep I=PA=cε0E022 the same. Then use the proportion of area A in the diagram to distance squared to find the distance that produces the calculated change in area.

interactions.teaches: As the receiving patch moves farther along the same ray bundle, the intercepted square grows with r squared, so the same transmitted power is spread over a larger area

interactions.label: Overlay
interactions.teaches: The geometric area increase and the inverse-square intensity decrease are the same relationship viewed from opposite sides: I is proportional to 1/A

demo_steps.title: Near receiving patch
demo_steps.narration: At r1 the same narrow bundle of rays cuts out the small square area A1. The patch is close to the radio source, so the received intensity is taken as I1.

demo_steps.title: Move the patch outward
demo_steps.narration: Dragging the patch to r2 keeps it inside the same four rays, but the square side length grows in proportion to r. The area at r2 is much larger than A1.

demo_steps.title: Read the intensity consequence
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the intensity overlay shows that the larger area means weaker received signal: I(r)/I1 = (r1/r)^2.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a long diagonal composition matching the source: radio source at lower left, ray bundle rising toward upper right. World-space source S = (0, 0, 0). Central beam unit direction approximately u = normalize(1.0, 0.52, 0.10). Near distance r1 = 2.2 units; far distance r2 = 5.0 units. Patch center C(r) = S + r*u. Near square side s1 = 0.45 units; variable patch side s(r) = s1*(r/r1), so at r2 the side is about 1.02 units. Area A1 = 0.2025 square units and A(r)/A1 = (r/r1)^2; at r2, A2/A1 is about 5.17. Normalized intensity I(r)/I1 = (r1/r)^2; at r2, I2/I1 is about 0.193. Square patches are perpendicular to the central ray, not screen-facing. Choose two local patch axes perpendicular to u so the patch appears as the same slanted parallelogram as the source figure, with its visible top edge leaning slightly down to the right and its side edges receding up-left/down-right. The four ray directions pass exactly through the four corners of the near square and the corresponding scaled corners of the current/far square. Draw solid blue rays from the source to the near A1 square; draw dashed blue rays from A1 to the far/current square, preserving the source figure's solid-near/dashed-far convention. The distance arrows run below and parallel to the central beam: r1 is the shorter upper dimension arrow ending under A1; r or r2 is the longer lower dimension arrow ending under the current patch. Use black double arrowheads and small angled endpoint ticks. Color palette: ray and patch outline blue #5aa6c7; patch fill pale blue #a9cdda at 55-70% opacity; dashed continuation rays same blue with dash pattern; labels/arrows black #111111; source dot black. Keep the figure on a white background with no coordinate axes.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement the receiving patch as a PlaneGeometry whose scale updates with distanceR while its orientation remains perpendicular to the beam direction. Recompute all four corner positions, ray segments, dashed continuation segments, dimension arrow endpoints, and label anchors whenever distanceR changes. Use CSS2D or sprite text for labels so A1, A2/A(r), r1, r/r2, and the numeric overlay remain readable. The intensity overlay can optionally tint the active patch from warmer/darker at r1 to paler/cooler at r2 while keeping the original blue style.
